items.title: More manic swings for Nvidia and other jittery AI stocks drag the U.S. market lower
items.description: The U.S. stock market is falling again Tuesday, as Nvidia and other stocks in the artificial intelligence industry swing following their sell-off from the day before.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Options trader Kirk Katzburg works on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange in New York, Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. (AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Yuki Iwamura</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: The U.S. stock market is falling again Tuesday, as Nvidia and other stocks in the artificial intelligence industry swing following their sell-off from the day before.
items.body:
NEW YORK — More manic swings for Nvidia and other stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry are dragging the U.S. market downward Tuesday.

The S&P 500 sank 1.1 per cent and at one point was on track for its first back-to-back losses of at least 1.5 per cent since March. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 779 points, or 1.5 per cent, as of 11:30 a.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was down 1.2 per cent.

The centre of the action was again Nvidia, which resumed its whipsaw moves. After flipping between modest gains and losses in the morning, it veered lower and dropped as much as 3.7 per cent before paring its loss to one per cent. The chip company is scheduled to deliver its latest earnings report after trading ends for the day. It will be the first time interim CEO Colette Kress speaks to Wall Street since taking over for Jensen Huang, the leather-jacketed star who became one of the most famous faces of the AI boom.

  • S&P 500 market updates here

The pressure is on Kress and Nvidia to show whether the company’s tremendous growth can continue following the stunning resignation of one of AI’s strongest influencers. Nvidia is creating a new board committee to oversee national security and global trade compliance following revelations that Huang had a relationship with an alleged spy for China.

Huang said on the X social-media network Tuesday that he would come back as CEO if “the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America.”

Other stocks in the AI industry likewise swung lower after giving up early-morning strength. Advanced Micro Devices went from an early gain of 1.6 per cent to a drop of 2.1 per cent. After an initial climb of 1.8 per cent, CoreWeave flipped to a loss of 1.3 per cent

AI-related stocks have been shaky for months because of a rolling chain of worries. At first, it was concerns that AI stock prices had broadly shot too high in their frenzy. Then it was worries that high interest rates would mean less borrowed money to fund further growth. More recently, it was concerns that Democratic victories in this month’s U.S. midterm elections could mean tougher regulations and restrictions on AI data centres.

  • Latest updates on artificial intelligence news here

Such stocks can almost single-handedly set the U.S. market’s course because they’ve grown into some of Wall Street’s most valuable and most influential.

Most of Wall Street was weak Tuesday, and Home Depot sank 2.3 per cent even though it reported profit for the latest quarter that edged past analysts’ expectations.

The retailer has been hampered by a housing market chilled by expensive mortgage rates, which have climbed with Treasury yields because of high oil prices, high inflation and other factors.

The 10-year Treasury yield climbed toward 5.15 per cent Tuesday morning from 5.12 per cent late Monday before later pulling back to 5.10 per cent. It erased its gains after the sharp drops for AI stocks pushed investors to herd into investments seen as safer bets.

In the morning, yields got support from a report showing an underlying measure of spending at U.S. retailers was stronger last month than economists expected. Such spending, along with big investments in AI, has helped the U.S. economy continue to grow despite frustration with high inflation.

Elsewhere on Wall Street, stocks of banks were lower amid concerns about how much pain the broad U.S. economy will feel from any pullback in AI-related spending.

JPMorgan Chase fell 2.1 per cent. A day before, a technical issue at the bank had slowed transactions for customers trying to use the Zelle payment system.

United Airlines had its own operational struggles, as a system outage lasted more than 90 minutes and forced the carrier to delay departing flights Monday. The outage came just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration’s network prompted a nationwide ground stop.

United’s stock lost 3.3 per cent, but that may have been due more to a rise in oil prices.

  • Latest updates on investing here

The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose one per cent to US$93.36. It’s been yo-yoing amid uncertainty about what will happen in the war with Iran.

The Walt Disney Co. helped limit Wall Street’s losses after rising 0.7 per cent. It reported stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected.

Stock prices generally tend to follow the path of corporate profits over the long term, depending on how interest rates behave. The big businesses across the S&P 500 index are on track to deliver earnings per share for the summer that are nearly 32 per cent higher than a year earlier, according to FactSet.

In stock markets abroad, indexes sank across much of Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi fell 2.6 per cent and dropped to its lowest closing level since February.

Stan Choe, The Associated Press

AP Writers Elaine Lai and Matt Ott contributed to this report.

items.title: ‘Are u really threatening to play China off the U.S.?’ Trump trade adviser asks PM Carney
items.description: A senior adviser to U.S. President Donald Trump shared harsh words against Canada’s potential auto trade expansion with China.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A senior adviser to U.S. President Donald Trump shared harsh words against Canada’s potential auto trade expansion with China. (Image credits: The Associated Press, The Canadian Press)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: A senior adviser to U.S. President Donald Trump shared harsh words against Canada’s potential auto trade expansion with China.
items.body:
A senior adviser to U.S. President Donald Trump shared harsh words against Canada’s potential auto trade expansion with China.

“Are u really threatening to play China off the U.S.? This is offensive in the extreme. You should be far more worried China is going to eat Canada alive--as it is already doing. Vancouver is not BC, its PRC,” said Peter Navarro, trade adviser to Trump, in what he called a “memo” to Prime Minister Mark Carney. Pete Hoekstra, Washington’s ambassador to Canada, reshared the post.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

Carney is in Shenzhen, China, this week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. On the sidelines of the event, he met with that country’s president, Xi Jinping. The two leaders agreed to lower tariffs on frozen pork and seafood, according to a readout of the exchange. More than 90 per cent of Canada-China trade is now on reduced tariffs, it said.

But if and how Canada and China expand auto trade has been a source of friction domestically and internationally. Navarro posted his statement in response to an Associated Press article quoting Carney’s suggestion that Canada could seek greater Chinese involvement in the domestic auto sector.

“We have the best autoworkers in the world, and we want them fully deployed … in an integrated north American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of U.S. trade actions.”

Auto tariffs

Throughout Trump’s second term in office, Canada and the U.S. have traded tariff barbs as part of a larger trade war.

U.S. President Donald Trump has imposed 25 per cent tariffs on auto imports from north of the border, with exemptions for content that fits into the two country’s existing trade deal, the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement. Canada retaliated with its own 25 per cent fees. In August, Trump threatened to raise tariffs on Canadian-made vehicles and auto parts to 50 per cent, effective Jan. 1, 2027.

The two countries share a deeply integrated auto manufacturing sector, which Carney called “the best result” for Canadian workers, businesses, and U.S. consumers. But the makeup of that sector depends on trade talks.

“Depending on where that settles, and it’s part of the trade negotiations … there will be other options, European options, Asian options. Of course, Chinese, Japanese,” he said.

Asked if he considers a potential auto deal with China as leverage in trade talks with the U.S., Carney said it was not, but “action, reaction.”

Trump has repeatedly said that the U.S. does not need Canadian-manufactured automobiles. He’s been forthright with his intention to reshore auto manufacturing within the United States, using tariffs as a lever to carry out that vision.

North of the border, Stellantis, a key player in that cross-border manufacturing chain, is reducing its footprint.

Stellantis had plans to retool its Brampton, Ont., assembly plant to produce the Jeep Compass electric SUV. The company halted that work after Trump began rolling out tariffs in 2025. It later said that production line would move to Illinois as part of its US$13-billion plan to expand U.S. production by 50 per cent.

Speaking alongside striking workers on Monday, NDP Leader Avi Lewis called the plant an essential piece of Canada’s industrial economy.

“Once we lose this industrial capacity, it is gone. It doesn’t come back. This tariff war is an attack on Canada and Donald Trump wants to de-industrialize this country,” he said.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has called on Carney to fire Industry Minister Melanie Joly over her handling of the Stellantis plant, which could soon be sold to Canadian armoured vehicle manufacturer Roshel.

Canada open to Chinese business

The federal government appears open to Chinese EVs being manufactured in Canada.

In June, after meeting with four Chinese car manufacturers, Joly told reporters that all the companies she met with are “willing to explore creating joint ventures in Canada in order to produce in Canada.”

The minister stipulated any arrangement would have to meet conditions, including a localized supply chain and Canadian control of the joint venture.

International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu visited one of those Chinese automakers, Chery, and posted online that he had done so “to discuss their upcoming models and hear about their plans to introduce affordable EVs to Canadians.”

In January, Carney announced a deal with Beijing to allow up to 49,000 Chinese EVs into Canada each year at a 6.1 per cent tariff. Canada had previously imposed a 100 per cent tariff in line with U.S. levies. In exchange, China would drop its tariffs on a number of Canadian agriculture products, including canola seeds and meal, some seafood and peas.

Since then, Canadian exports to China have surged.

Statistics Canada reported this week that, in the first nine months of 2026, Canada’s exports rose 40 per cent to reach $33.5 billion – a rate that far outpaces growth in exports to any other nation, according to the federal government.

China’s exports to Canada, in contrast, did not grow at the same rate. Between January and September, Canada imported $68.8 billion in Chinese goods, about $700 million more than in the same period a year earlier.

Navarro’s note mirrors similar language from Trump, who said in January that China would “’eat them up’ within the first year” of expanded trade.

“China is successfully and completely taking over the once Great Country of Canada. So sad to see it happen. I only hope they leave Ice Hockey alone!” he also wrote on Truth Social.

With files from CTV News’ Vassy Kapelos and Marieke Walsh, and The Canadian Press

items.title: Trump administration moves to block China from indirect access to American AI technology
items.description: The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China’s abilities to use U.S. chips to train their best artificial intelligence models.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick speaks at a campaign rally, Oct. 13, 2026, in Wasilla, Alaska. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon, File)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Alex Brandon</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China’s abilities to use U.S. chips to train their best artificial intelligence models.
items.body:
WASHINGTON -- The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China’s abilities to use U.S. chips to train their best artificial intelligence models.

Last week, Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO following scrutiny of his ties to a Chinese executive who used to lead Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which is suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls. The company provides computing power to Chinese companies using chips housed in Southeast Asian data centers, including facilities in Malaysia.

“The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centres in third countries,” the Bureau of Industry and Security under the Commerce Department said in issuing the rule that took effect immediately.

The rule came on the same day U.S. President Donald Trump departed for a trip to Asia, where he expects to meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the third time this year amid a fragile truce on trade.

Under the new rule, overseas data centers that serve companies in countries including China, Russia, Iran and Cuba are required to identify their end users. There also will be additional licensing requirements for sales of chips for Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil -- countries that “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion” to unauthorized destinations, the rule says.

In Beijing, China’s foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun accused Washington of arbitrarily interfering with China’s trade and technological cooperation with other countries and suppressing the development of China’s high-tech industries.

“This is a typical example of economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction, runs counter to the common understanding between the two sides,” he told reporter, adding that it infringes upon the rights of Chinese companies and disrupts the stability of global supply chains.

He said China would take necessary measures to safeguard its interests.

The U.S. bans sales of the country’s most advanced AI chips to China, seeking to maintain an edge in its rivalry with China for predominance in artificial intelligence. However, many lawmakers and policymakers believe the country’s export control rules are not tough enough and filled with loopholes such as cloud computing that allows China to rent processing power built on American technology.

Last year, U.S. Rep. Michael Lawler, a New York Republican, introduced a bill to broaden the U.S. export controls to include remote access. He told Congress “physical export controls” under current rules do not apply to remote access, allowing China to “access our tech through the cloud” and giving it “a real tool to sidestep” U.S. export restrictions. The bill has passed the House.

In the Senate, lawmakers also are seeking tougher legislation to prevent China from accessing advanced U.S. chip and AI technologies. Bills include proposals that would let Congress review licences to sell advanced AI chips to China, ask the Department of Commerce to track AI chips to ensure they are not diverted to unauthorized regions, and compel U.S. allies such as the Netherlands and Japan to match U.S. restrictions on exports to Chinese chipmakers.

Last week, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick came under pressure when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the Commerce Department was late to place restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to Megaspeed.

On Monday, Trump acknowledged tension between Treasury and Commerce on the matter. He suggested that Lutnick may have delayed placing the export restrictions to avoid a “blow up” in the fragile U.S.-China relationship.

“We’re having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it, Trump said.

In a joint statement late Monday by the Commerce and Justice departments, it said Commerce initiated an investigation into Megaspeed for potential export control violations in 2024, which was followed by requests to Nvidia for records in May 2025 related to sales to Megaspeed. The following month, it said, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list, and agents from the Commerce Department in conjunction with Singapore law enforcement conducted on-site checks of Megaspeed and interviewed Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang. The Justice Department then took the lead role in the criminal probe of Megaspeed, the statement said.

“The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security working together will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred,” the statement said.

Last week, the Singapore government confirmed that it had investigated Megaspeed over “potential false declarations” involving servers that were exported through Singapore to Malaysia but might have “subsequently been routed from Malaysia to another destination, contrary to declaration made in Singapore.”

The Malaysian government also said last week that it was investigating if chips brought into Malaysia have been re-exported to other countries as permitted by its own law.

“Malaysia welcomes investment in data centers and technology, but will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls,” read the Friday statement by Malaysia’s Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry.

items._ogDesc: Key U.S. House and Congress lawmakers said Tuesday that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has voluntarily agreed to appear for transcribed interviews
items.body:
WASHINGTON — Key U.S. House and Congress lawmakers said Tuesday that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has voluntarily agreed to appear for transcribed interviews as the chipmaker faces intensifying national security scrutiny over sales of its advanced computer chips.

Huang will appear before the committees on Dec. 1, followed by the company’s general counsel, Tim Teter, on Dec. 2.

“We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security,” said a statement from the chairmen of three House committees with oversight over China and intelligence issues.

“The American people need answers on Mr. Huang and Nvidia’s role in allowing dangerous PRC actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal,” the lawmakers said, referring to the People’s Republic of China.

Also Tuesday, Nvidia said it’s creating a new board committee to oversee national security and global trade compliance following revelations that Huang had an extramarital affair with an alleged spy for China.

Nvidia said the National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee will be responsible for oversight of national security policies and compliance with export controls.

  • Latest updates on company news here

Nvidia’s advanced chips are in high demand because they’re essential for cloud computing and data centres that underpin the artificial intelligence boom, but they face restrictions on their sale to China.

The committee will meet at least once every quarter and have three members from Nvidia’s board of directors. It will work with independent third-party experts as it oversees efforts to enhance the company’s existing national security and global trade compliance team.

“We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation,” Chairman Harvey Jones said in a statement.

  • Latest updates on artificial intelligence news here

U.S. President Donald Trump said it was “good” that Nvidia had created a national security and export control oversight committee shortly after arriving in the Philippines on Tuesday evening.

“Yes, that’s a good idea. It’s a great company,” Trump said during a photo opportunity in Manila with the leaders of Australia, India and Japan. “It’s a great idea.”

Huang was forced to resign as Nvidia’s CEO last week following scrutiny of his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who used to lead Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed International, which is suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of the U.S. export controls.

Kevin Freking, The Associated Press

AP writers Kelvin Chan in London, Darlene Superville and Kevin Freking in Washington, contributed to this report.

items._ogDesc: The parliamentary budget officer is questioning the federal government’s vow to spend less and invest more.
items.body:
OTTAWA — The parliamentary budget officer is questioning the federal government’s vow to spend less and invest more.

In a series of reports released today scrutinizing the federal budget, PBO Annette Ryan says the Liberal government’s overall fiscal situation is a bit rosier than the forecast in Ottawa’s last spending update in the spring.

But Ryan says the government has used up 96 per cent of the new fiscal room from higher-than-expected revenues through fresh spending commitments, instead of reducing the deficit.

The PBO projects the cost of federal measures is $331.6 billion higher in the three spending plans tabled so far under Prime Minister Mark Carney.

Most of that spending is reserved for the day-to-day operations of government, not the kind of capital spending Carney has promised to prioritize.

While the government laid out a path to meet its fiscal anchors in Budget 2026, the PBO warns those margins are narrow.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

items.title: Spending growth slowed at U.S. retail stores in October as high prices give shoppers pause
items.description: U.S. shoppers increased spending more slowly in October as economic uncertainty and high prices led more Americans to pull back on a variety of purchases.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Shoppers walk an aisle at a grocery store in the Dallas suburb of Richardson, Texas, Friday, Oct. 23, 2026. (AP Photo/LM Otero)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Lm Otero</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: U.S. shoppers increased spending more slowly in October as economic uncertainty and high prices led more Americans to pull back on a variety of purchases.
items.body:
NEW YORK — U.S. shoppers increased spending more slowly in October as economic uncertainty and high prices led more Americans to pull back on a variety of purchases from cars to clothing and furniture, even their hobbies, ahead of the unofficial start to the holiday shopping season.

Retail sales rose 0.2 per cent in October, down from a 0.8 per cent gain in September, according to the Commerce Department’s report released Tuesday.

Sales at gas stations rose 1.5 per cent last month after spiking 30.3 per cent in September. Excluding gas stations, retail sales rose just 0.1 per cent.

  • Latest updates on international news here

Overall retail sales were pulled down by decline in sales at motor vehicle and parts dealers. Auto vehicles and parts dealers had a 1.6 per cent drop in sales in October, reversing a 1.3 per cent increase in September. Excluding that sector, retail sales rose 0.6 per cent.

Adjusting for higher prices, consumer spending was “negative,” according to Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union. The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4 per cent in October, according to data released last week, hotter than expected.

“The cautious consumer is back,” Long wrote Tuesday. “October retail sales were tepid. Budgets are tight for many households.”

She noted the drop in gas prices in November will help free up some much-needed cash this holiday season, but middle-class and moderate-income households are “feeling the strain.”

Yet even with a recent decline in gas prices, a gallon still costs nearly 20 per cent more than at this time last year.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

Business was down at multiple types of businesses, including clothing stores and furniture and home furnishing retailers, last month, according to the report. Even the sporting goods, musical instruments, books and hobby store sector struggled with a decline in sales. That sector had been strong this past spring and summer as shoppers focus on fun little splurges, Long noted.

One of the bright spots was online retailers, which saw a boost from a two-day Amazon Prime Day event, which took place in early October. That sector was up 1.2 per cent.

The data offers only a snapshot of consumer spending and doesn’t include activities like travel and hotel stays. But the lone services category – restaurants registered a 0.2 per cent increase.

Still, the so-called control group—which excludes food services, autos, building materials and gas station sales and is used to calculate economic growth—rose a solid 0.6 per cent.

Higher energy prices are ricocheting into other parts of the economy, with airfares, public transportation and shipping all jumping in price. Grocery prices, for example, increased 0.4 per cent, a painful uptick after years of increases, according to new Labor Department data.

Massive investments in artificial intelligence have exacerbated inflation by driving up computer chip prices and, in turn, prices for laptops, phones and other consumer electronics.

Retailers are preparing for a surge in business over the Thanksgiving weekend, the unofficial start of the holiday shopping period. Stores have heavily advertised deals to lure customers who increasingly buy when they think prices have dropped.

  • Trade War coverage on BNNBloomberg.ca

Companies like Kohl’s and Target and Walmart are trying to drive the affordability message home through marketing.

Target said it’s offering more than 8,000 new gifts for the winter holidays, with more than half exclusive to the retailer. Most of the new holiday items at Target are US$20 or less, including thousands of items that are priced at US$5 and under. Kohl’s has increased the number of gift sets across different types of merchandise.

Americans, despite the rising cost of credit, continue to rely on cards to finance spending, and credit experts say that defaults have been stable.

“More Americans are carrying credit cards than ever, and they’re handling them well,” said Charles Wise, head of global research and consulting at the credit reporting agency TransUnion.

Wise noted that outstanding credit card balances as of last month hit US$1.17 trillion, up 5.1 per cent from the year-ago period, based on data covering 178.5 million consumers who held an active credit card as of last month. Yet serious delinquency rates held steady, he said.

That signals that “consumers remain disciplined borrowers heading into the holidays,” he added.

Anne D’Innocenzio, The Associated Press

items._ogDesc: Some telecommunications analysts are casting doubt that a merger between Quebecor Inc. and Telus Corp. would be able to clear all regulatory hurdles.
items.body:
Some telecommunications analysts are casting doubt that a proposed merger between Quebecor Inc. and Telus Corp. would be able to clear all regulatory hurdles and make it to the finish line.

Quebecor revealed Monday it is proposing a $31-billion takeover of Telus in a cash-and-stock deal, however Telus says it sees “serious concerns” with the offer, topped by questions on how it would pass regulatory scrutiny.

RBC analyst Drew McReynolds says he believes there is a “low probability” of the companies joining forces under the current regulatory environment, and that achieving the required government approvals “without material remedies appears to us to be a non-starter.”

Desjardins analyst Jerome Dubreuil says that although there’s a “compelling long-term strategic rationale” for a potential merger, it would face a “challenging” road.

  • Latest updates on company news here

Telus has not accepted the proposal and says it is continuing to review the bid, but a potential agreement would likely prompt reviews by the Competition Bureau, the CRTC and Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said in a statement on Monday that the transaction will be “rigorously reviewed.”

“In the face of accelerating technological change, global instability and ongoing cost-of-living pressures, the Government of Canada will relentlessly prioritize the best interests of Canadians and Canadian sovereignty,” she said.

Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press

items.title: David Beckham sues for US$41 million after his fragrance is sold in gas stations and discount stores
items.description: A dispute over the sale of David Beckham perfumes has struck a sour note with the soccer star turned style icon.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[FILE -David Beckham poses with his new star during a ceremony on the Hollywood Walk of Fame on June 12, 2026, in Los Angeles. (AP Photo/Chris Pizzello, File)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Chris Pizzello</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: A dispute over the sale of David Beckham perfumes has struck a sour note with the soccer star turned style icon.
items.body:
LONDON — A dispute over the sale of David Beckham perfumes has struck a sour note with the soccer star turned style icon.

Beckham’s commercial company is suing a beauty firm after his “luxury” fragrances were allegedly found for sale in discount stores and a gas station bargain bin.

DB Ventures has filed a claim in the New York Supreme Court against German beauty group Coty, which makes and distributes a range of Beckham-branded fragrances and toiletries. They include the Classic and Instinct lines and the eaux de toilette Intimately and Exquisite Leather.

The claim argues that Beckham’s “world-renowned global brand is synonymous with excellence and refinement,” and “David Beckham products are a symbol of everyday luxury.”

“Imagine, then, the shock and dismay experienced when DB Ventures discovered that David Beckham products were being offered for sale in a gas station,” the legal document says. “How could this possibly have happened? Desperation and greed.”

Lawyers for DB Ventures allege that Beckham-branded products “ended up in the bargain bin inside a gas station” and at British budget retailer Poundland, “allowing the product to be sold for dollar store prices and associating the David Beckham brand with cheap, discount products.”

DB Ventures is seeking at least US$41 million in damages for breach of its licensing agreement.

Coty has asked a judge to dismiss the lawsuit, which was filed in April. The company argues that New York courts have no jurisdiction in the case, and says DB Ventures is using the claim to “manufacture its early exit” from its licensing deal and hand over the Beckham contracts to another firm, Interparfums.

The company told The Associated Press on Tuesday that “Coty strongly disputes the claims and has asked the court to dismiss them. As this is an ongoing legal matter, we will not comment further.”

DB Ventures didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Beckham, who played for a number of clubs including Manchester United and Real Madrid and captained the England men’s national team, parlayed success on the pitch into a lucrative business career that includes co-ownership of soccer team Inter Miami. He was knighted last year by King Charles III, becoming Sir David.

He also has had a very public persona as a fashion model, “Bend It Like Beckham” movie muse and is husband to Spice Girl-turned-fashion designer Victoria “Posh Spice” Beckham. The couple have four children.

The Sunday Times Rich List earlier this year estimated the Beckhams’ wealth at almost 1.2 billion pounds (US$1.58 billion).

items.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney secured new trade concessions from China that will benefit Canadian pork and seafood producers, while tensions over his push to attract Chinese automakers to invest in Canada continued to complicate efforts to reset relations with Beijing.

THE CANADIAN PRESS/Adrian Wyld]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Adrian Wyld</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Prime Minister Mark Carney secured new trade concessions from China that will benefit Canadian pork and seafood producers, while tensions over his push to attract Chinese automakers to invest in Canada continued to complicate efforts to reset relations with Beijing.
items.body:
SHENZHEN, China — Prime Minister Mark Carney secured new trade concessions from China that will benefit Canadian pork and seafood producers, while tensions over his push to attract Chinese automakers to invest in Canada continued to complicate efforts to reset relations with Beijing.

Meeting Chinese President Xi Jinping on Tuesday as the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit got underway, Carney heard Xi declare that China’s relationship with Canada had “fully resumed.”

  • ‘Are u really threatening to play China off the U.S.?’ Trump trade adviser asks PM Carney
  • Carney and Sheinbaum meet at summit in China, as both navigate Trump’s tumult
  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

The two countries announced measures to reduce tariffs on a range of Canadian goods, with pork and seafood producers among the biggest beneficiaries.

Canadian officials valued the extended tariff relief at more than $400 million, including $116 million in frozen pork cuts, $96 million in Greenland halibut, and various frozen cold-water prawns and shrimp.

“China is one of the most critical markets for pork processors and exporters,” said Kyle Larkin, president and CEO of the Canadian Meat Council, speaking to Canadian reporters in Shenzhen.

“It’s really great news for the Canadian pork industry, and more importantly for a thousand farmers and workers in Canada,” said Karan Sangfai, CEO of HyLife, one of Canada’s top pork producers.

Canadian officials were measured in describing the progress, which Carney has characterized as a “warming” of relations after years of tension, including China’s detention of Michael Spavor and Michael Kovrig.

“In total, now we are just shy of $8-billion worth of Canadian exports back into the Chinese marketplace,” said Kody Blois, parliamentary secretary to the prime minister.

He said agreements were also reached for market access to geoduck and mollusk.

“This is a major seafood market and one of the largest for us in the world, and we needed to make sure we get that market access back.”

Chinese EVs

The trade gains are part of Carney’s broader effort to diversify Canada’s economy and reduce its reliance on the United States.

Since his visit to Beijing in January 2026, the two countries have made progress on several trade issues. Canadian merchandise exports to China rose 31.4 per cent in the first half of 2026 to $21.5 billion, according to Global Affairs Canada. Crude oil shipments to China have also increased by approximately 37 per cent this year.

China has suspended additional tariffs on Canadian canola meal, peas, lobster and crab, with both countries agreeing on Nov. 4 to extend those market-access concessions through the end of 2028. China has also restored access for Canadian beef from 20 registered meat establishments.

But the push to deepen trade ties has a more contentious dimension: Carney wants Chinese automakers to consider investing in Canadian manufacturing, potentially creating opportunities for autoworkers affected by U.S. tariffs.

There was no new announcement on Chinese electric vehicles entering Canada, with the two countries maintaining the agreement reached in January 2026.

“We have the best autoworkers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Phnom Penh, Cambodia. “If they are not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities.”

Peter Navarro, the White House trade adviser, responded to Carney’s comments on social media.

“Are u really threatening to play China off the U.S.? This is offensive in the extreme. You should be far more worried China is going to eat Canada alive,” Navarro wrote.

Carney has said any Chinese automotive investment in Canada must involve genuine domestic manufacturing, rather than simply assembling vehicles from imported Chinese parts.

“It’s not just about kit cars. There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved,” he said.

The January agreement opened the Canadian market to a limited number of Chinese electric vehicles. Canada replaced its previous 100 per cent surtax with the standard 6.1 per cent most-favoured-nation tariff, subject to an annual quota of 49,000 vehicles.

Beyond trade, the relationship remains complicated by disagreements over foreign interference, cybersecurity, human rights and national security. Carney has said closer economic engagement with China does not mean Canada is setting aside those concerns.

For Carney, the challenge is to expand Canada’s access to the Chinese market while protecting domestic industries and managing an increasingly complicated relationship with its largest trading partner, the United States.

items.title: Firm Capital Buys Highlight Of Mississauga Project Under Creditor Protection For $74.3M
items.description:
A large condo project in Mississauga that became insolvent and was placed under creditor protection mid-construction over four years ago has officially been sold, according to filings in Ontario Superior Court.

The project is known as Highlight of Mississauga and is located at 4064, 4070, and 4078 Dixie Road, right across the street from Rockwood Mall in Mississauga.

The developer was a company called Hazelton Development Corporation (HDC) and the project website identifies an individual named Du Zhixian as the company’s President. Court documents also refer to him as Joe Du, and note that the company is majority-owned by “a prominent construction family in China.”

For the site, Hazelton Development Corporation was developing a 14-storey project with 265 strata units, including both condos and townhomes. Presales launched around May 2018 and 261 of 265 units were pre-sold, generating a total of $111,633,085 in revenue.

Construction commenced in September 2019 and completion was targeted for April 2021, but the project faced delays and liquidity issues that resulted in HDC seeking out creditor protection under the federal Companies’ Creditors Arrangement Act (CCAA) in April 2022, by which construction had reached Level 12.

The Debts

For the project, Hazelton took out a first-ranking mortgage with Meridian Credit Union in May 2019 for a construction loan with a principal amount of up to $50 million, plus a stand-by letter of credit facility up to $2 million.

It also took out a second mortgage with Centurion Mortgage Capital Corporation — which was folded into Centurion Asset Management in 2024 — for a construction facility of up to $19.9 million, plus a cost-overrun facility up to $3.5 million.

As of the time of their filing, HDC owed approximately $20,694,142 to Meridian and $20,673,626 to Centurion, for a total of $41,367,768, with interest continuing to accrue.

According to HDC, certain shareholders also loaned HDC approximately $6.35 million between September 2019 and March 2022, and a company called Triumph Eastern Investments Inc. also advanced six loans between October 2021 and March 2022.

Various amounts were also owed to contractors.

The Insolvency

Hazelton Development Corporation said they faced trouble from the onset as the COVID-19 pandemic hit just a few months after construction commenced. In March 2020, they notified purchasers that the project would be delayed. Construction later resumed, but HDC had to issue additional delay notices in May 2021, November 2021, January 2022, and March 2022.

“The initial construction budget for the Project was $101,183,823,” said HDC. “By November 2021, under previous management, the forecasted construction budget had increased by $11,672,011 to $113,669,237. These increases were due to, among other things: two significant delays on account of Covid-19 lock-downs, an increased level of supervision and project management, substantial increases to the hard costs budget for concrete, masonry, mechanical equipment and electrical work, and various material increases to the soft costs budget.”

Construction loan agreements often include obligations that borrowers maintain a minimum debt-to-equity ratio, but although HDC was able to raise additional equity from shareholders, it was not enough to satisfy Meridian’s requirement, and the lender ceased advances in July 2021, forcing HDC to rely on Centurion and buyer deposits.

In March 2022, the Du family bought out a group of shareholders, which gave them an 80% stake in HDC, and brought in new management to stabilize the project. A month later, in April 2022, HDC filed for creditor protection.

The Highlight of Mississauga as of March 2026. (Grant Thornton)

Under Creditor Protection

In July 2022, Toronto-based non-bank lender Firm Capital (TSX: FC) emerged as a sponsor and agreed to loan up to $80 million to pay off various debts and finance the construction of Highlight of Mississauga. The plan was approved, and construction then resumed.

In February 2023, the court then granted an order allowing the presale purchasers to be given two options. The first option would allow them to carry on with the purchase under revised terms, while the second option would terminate the presale agreement and see the buyer be compensated for their deposit with a 12% premium.

Although there were disputes with contractors and various other delays, construction continued and reached approximately 92.6% completion by February 2026, when the court-appointed Monitor said that “The ongoing deficiencies, construction challenges, weather-related delays, rising completion costs, and the Company’s funding constraints, have resulted in further delays to completion” and that “The Monitor understands that completion of the Project may no longer be feasible.”

By then, most of the presale purchasers had taken the compensation option and there were 197 unsold units. Lien claims by contractors had also continued to pile up, totalling to $10,802,325.

The Sale

The court-ordered sales process commenced in late-February. According to a report prepared by the Monitor, 15 parties signed confidentiality agreements and five toured the site. One party submitted a letter of intent in June, but reduced their offer during negotiations the following month, citing higher-than-anticipated expected taxes.

The Monitor then engaged other bidders, but could not find a better offer. Feedback from the market was that the project was better suited as a rental building, that the cost to complete was anywhere from $15 million to $30 million, and that the required remedial work was an added level of uncertainty.

“When it became apparent that there would be no unconditional bids,” said the Monitor, Firm Capital then began discussions to buy the project themselves through a reverse vesting order that would see them buy the shares of Hazelton Development Corporation — a share sale — instead of directly buying the real estate. Firm Capital’s purchase agreement also required that the remaining 48 presale contracts be terminated.

The purchase price is equivalent to the sum of various floating amounts, totalling to around $73.5 million, plus $802,000 in cash consideration, for a total of around $74.3 million estimated at September 30, 2026.

The sale approval court hearing was originally scheduled for October 1, but was then delayed due to various stakeholders raising objections. The hearing was delayed to October 22, then October 26, before it was finally approved by the Ontario Superior Court on November 4.

items.body:
OTTAWA — The Canadian Real Estate Association says October home sales crept up slightly from September but were still down more than 10 per cent from a year ago.

The organization says home sales last month totalled 37,827, down 10.6 per cent from October 2025.

On a seasonally adjusted basis, activity edged up 0.3 per cent compared with September.

The national average sale price in October ticked down 1.6 per cent from a year ago to $678,584.

New listings fell 5.5 per cent to 75,814, but on a seasonally adjusted basis, were up 0.8 per cent from the month before and outpaced sales activity.

CREA chair Garry Bhaura says the numbers signal there's been only a slight slowdown in housing activity from the summer to the fall, even as interest rates rose in late October.

“With the market moving into its traditionally quieter months, now is a great time to shift into planning mode for 2027," Bhaura said in a statement.

CREA said there were about 197,000 properties listed for sale on all Canadian MLS systems at the end of October, up slightly from the long-term average of 190,000.

It said there were five months of inventory on a national basis at the end of October, up slightly from the summer.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

items._ogDesc: Canadian inflation held at 3.1% in October, while property taxes rose 3.8%, outpacing overall price growth as Ontario tax arrears climbed.
items.body:
Canada’s headline inflation remains elevated, but at least it didn’t get worse. Statistics Canada (StatCan) data shows annual headline CPI growth held at 3.1% in October. The lack of acceleration would be good news if not for broadening inflation. Core measures didn’t clarify much this month, but one thing was clear—property taxes are still ripping while arrears climb.

Canadian Inflation Holds At 3.1%, Tamed By Cooling Gas Prices

Annual CPI growth rate.

Annual growth of CPI held at 3.1% in October, remaining elevated but unchanged from September. Helping to tame growth was a deceleration in gasoline prices, which fell 2.5% in the month but were up 30.9% from last year. The agency also notes that annual declines for cellphone plans (-6.2%) helped, though prices may not be lower. Cell phone plans have been a persistent downward pressure due to methodology, not because people are paying less.

Hard Core? Canada’s “Stable” Core CPI Measures Moved Lower, Higher, and Stalled

Canada’s Core CPI measures are designed to provide some clarity, and minimize headline volatility. Unfortunately, Canada’s three big core measures all told a different story last month.

CPI median’s annual growth was unchanged at 2.0%. The core measure tracks the midpoint of price changes, weighted by spending.

CPI-trim slowed from 1.9% to 1.8% in October. This measure excludes the largest upward and downward movements, ideally eliminating the volatility. In practice, prices take the elevator up and the stairs down. As a result, much larger price surges can be neutralized by much smaller declines.

CPI-common accelerated to 2.5% y/y in October, up from 2.4% in September. This measure tracks price movements across categories, filtering out fluctuations for individual items.

No measure is perfect, and the mixed direction reveals how flawed the shift to annual re-indexing has been. The agency’s Census intervals are spaced out to minimize the volatility of resource allocation. However, StatCan argues the pricing of those resources needs to be re-indexed annually.

Canadian Property Tax Growth Slows, But Still Faster Than Inflation

Annual growth of property taxes and special charges.

Every October StatCan’s CPI reports property taxes and other special charges. The segment saw prices rise 3.8% from last year, down from 5.6% reported in 2025. Slower than recent years, but it’s coming down from the sharpest surge since the early ’90s. At the same time, it’s nearly double the BoC’s target rate of inflation, and well above its upper bound of tolerance.

Slower-but-still-elevated property tax and special charges are also unlikely to feel like relief. The 3.3% annual growth in Ontario follows last year’s 5.5% jump. It’s been accompanied by a sharp rise in property tax arrears. Recent filings in the region reveal a property tax arrears rate of up to 11.9% in its largest municipalities.

items.title: When will Canada’s housing market finally bounce back?
items.description: It’s been more of the same for the Canadian housing outlook in 2026. Will 2027 bring a change?
items.content: <p>It’s been more of the same for the Canadian housing outlook in 2026. Will 2027 bring a change?</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639298402582987630.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: It’s been more of the same for the Canadian housing outlook in 2026. Will 2027 bring a change?
items.body:
Fall activity in Canada’s housing market has remained muted as affordability challenges and economic unease continue to roil the sector, with little chance of a pickup in momentum before the end of 2026.

A recent analysis by RBC Economics described a housing market recovery as “shaky at best” over the past several weeks, marked by even or declining home values and virtually no uptick in sales.

The main reasons for that will come as no surprise to mortgage market watchers: the trade war with the US is still rumbling on, while interest rates have been on the up and immigration numbers have dwindled.

There’s been some room for optimism on the trade front in November, with prime minister Mark Carney and US president Donald Trump suggesting both sides were working towards an agreement to end the tariff dispute.

But the combination of the Bank of Canada’s recent interest rate increase and continued economic turbulence south of the border mean a recovery in the housing and mortgage markets could still be some distance away, according to Ownright co-founder and chief operating officer Joel Fox.

“Until we see a rate drop, I’d be quite surprised if we started to see year-over-year growth in the market,” Fox told Canadian Mortgage Professional. “The rate hike just really cemented that.”

US election provides ‘glimmer of hope’ but obstacles remain

The BoC’s latest decision saw it move off the sidelines for the first time in over three years, raising rates by 25 basis points as inflation fears harden amid the ongoing US-Iran conflict.

Still, Fox acknowledged reasons for guarded optimism following the US midterm election results, which saw the Democratic Party reclaim both the House and Senate and stirred hopes of renewed efforts to bring the trade conflict to a close.

But the unpredictable nature of US politics and the current administration also means it’s too soon to say whether a definitive end to tariff tensions is near, he added.

“There’s a glimmer of hope that we might be able to get to something with the US, which I think both they and us really, really want to see happen,” he said. “That said, we’ve of course seen that before – and then it all went belly up fast.”

Expectations continue to ramp down for Canada’s housing market

The sluggish pace of homebuying activity and continuing economic anxiety have seen forecasters including the Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA) adjust their expectations for the housing market this year and next.

In October, the association revealed it had lowered its home sales forecast for the third quarter in a row, slashing 18,806 sales from its July expectations and now projecting overall sales for the year to slip 5.2% from 2025.

CREA said it now expected national average 2026 home prices to increase at a slower pace than previously anticipated, with forecasts of a slightly improved outlook for next year “predicated on slow but positive economic growth, the resumption of higher population growth, and more certainty for borrowers around the path for interest rates.”

Those factors, the association said, should move pent-up demand off the sidelines even as borrowing costs continue to jump.

Unsurprisingly, real estate and mortgage industry sentiment has also adjusted, with the belief that a market bounce-back was just around the corner now giving way to a less bullish approach. Fox said he’s noticed that among referral partners including real estate agents and mortgage brokers.

“Within the past two or three months, that optimism just doesn’t seem to be there – which is shocking, because [it’s] always felt like it’s been there,” he said.

While the COVID-19 pandemic marked a lucrative time to be employed in Canadian real estate, bringing with it a flood of new entrants into the realtor profession, many of those who joined during that era are now having second thoughts about their future.

“The COVID boom brought a lot of realtors into the market, and everything that’s happened since then is continuing to drive folks out,” he said. “You’ve got professionals in the space that are finding a way to work in this market – but there’s just not enough business to go around for everyone else.”

items.content: <p>Mortgage agent on how she’s helping new buyers break into the market</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0343_639304466007678370.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Mortgage agent on how she’s helping new buyers break into the market
items.body:
First-time buyers who spent years on the sidelines are finally getting into the market as affordability improves and purchase competition eases. We caught up with Mortgage Powered Financial Group mortgage agent Sarita Free at MortgageFest to hear how she’s helping borrowers navigate the current environment.

[00:00] They're finally able to break into the market and stay in their hometown where they've grown up and not have to go elsewhere. It's huge. It helps them qualify for a little bit more. Again, work your book, know your clients. Nothing's just going to be handed to you. So, 2027 is going to be what you make it as a broker.

[00:26] Fergal McAlinden: All right. Well, next up we have our first mortgage agent of the day. We've talked only with lenders so far. So, today we're really happy to have Sarita Free with Mortgage Powered Financial Group.

[00:36] Sarita Free: Yep. It's a mouthful, but you got it.

[00:39] Fergal McAlinden: Good stuff. Is it useful for you as an agent to speak with lenders, get some facetime? I mean, there's a lot of them here today. What type of conversation have you been having?

[00:46] Sarita Free: Well, to be quite honest, I haven't been able to get right in. I'd like to go see some of the tech companies to be fully transparent. Anything that makes my job easier, especially with AI coming out and just stuff to streamline my process.

[01:00] Fergal McAlinden: How about the market so far this year, 2026? We all know it's been an interesting outlook for agents and lenders and everyone. How are you navigating it and what are some of the main things you've been seeing?

[01:11] Sarita Free: Obviously I think my market is special. I'm in Norfolk County, Ontario, and our prices have been pretty stable. A lot of my clients are first-time home buyers and they've finally been able to break in. I am seeing a lot more alternative files on my desk, which is fitting because I'm moderating the alternative panel later. [laughter]

[01:28] Fergal McAlinden: For first-time home buyers, I know for a lot of them this has been kind of the light at the end of the tunnel after what we've been seeing over the past few years. Suddenly, they're in a position to buy. Has that been a big change for you this year?

[01:38] Sarita Free: My book typically has been a lot of first-time home buyers, but yes, this year I'm finding that they're finally able to get into the market. Norfolk County has some great home ownership programs as well. And again, with the 30-year amortization that we can now go to, I find a lot of my buyers that have been on the sidelines, they're finally able to break into the market and stay in their hometown where they've grown up and not have to go elsewhere.

[02:04] Which is huge. Norfolk County, again, it's a special place.

[02:06] Fergal McAlinden: For sure. And that's something that we haven't always seen. People looking to buy have had to go further afield. They haven't been able to stay where they are.

[02:13] Sarita Free: Like a couple of years ago when there were multiple offers and bidding wars. It was so disheartening to have these conversations with people whose family has been in our county for decades and them not being able to break in. So, this year has been really heartwarming and last year, too.

[02:32] Fergal McAlinden: That 30-year amortization is something that I wanted to ask you about. It's really interesting to hear that so many are using that. I know there was a little bit of skepticism about it when it was first unveiled, but every agent and broker that I've spoken to says that's been a really big game changer for buyers.

[02:46] Sarita Free: Yeah, it's huge. It helps them qualify for a little bit more. It makes the payments a little bit more manageable. So it's come in really handy. I'd like to see it in the insurable space. Maybe.

[02:59] Fergal McAlinden: We'll see.

[03:00] Sarita Free: We can hope.

[03:01] Fergal McAlinden: Anything else for first-time buyers? Any other kinds of trends across your desk when you're dealing with them? Are price points okay for them?

[03:09] Sarita Free: Yeah, I think price points are good right now. In more broader markets things have kind of leveled out. Norfolk County as well. I'm really passionate about Norfolk County. It's a smaller market and the majority of my book is there. So, it's a lot different than Toronto and the GTA, but yeah, prices are great and they've absolutely been able to get into the market. It's more affordable now.

items.description: Canada’s central bank kicks off its governor search as Macklem rules out a second term
items.content: <p>Canada’s central bank kicks off its governor search as Macklem rules out a second term</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639304443759641224.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Canada’s central bank kicks off its governor search as Macklem rules out a second term
items.body:
Tiff Macklem, the 10th Governor of the Bank of Canada, confirmed Monday he will not seek a second term when his seven-year mandate expires on June 2, 2027.

The Bank’s board has formed a search committee assisted by Zurich-based executive recruiting firm Egon Zehnder, with results expected by spring 2027.

The new governor will be formally appointed by Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne and Prime Minister Mark Carney — himself a former Bank of Canada governor — to take office on June 3, 2027.

“It has been the highlight of my career to serve as the 10th Governor of the Bank of Canada,” Macklem said.

“My time as Governor has seen Canada navigate a more fragmented, shock-prone world. The Bank has faced these challenges by acting decisively, by using sound judgment in the face of uncertainty, and by serving Canadians with humility and a steadfast commitment to its mandate.”

Macklem, 65, took the role on June 3, 2020, with the overnight rate already cut to 0.25% and an emergency bond-purchasing program underway.

His departure was widely expected; no governor had served a second term since 1980.

A legacy shaped by historic rate swings

The defining feature of Macklem’s tenure was Canada’s inflation fight. Consumer prices peaked at 8.1% in mid-2022, prompting one of the Bank’s most aggressive tightening cycles on record — 10 consecutive hikes over 16 months lifted the policy rate from 0.25% to 5%.

After cutting rates, the Bank raised again to 2.5% on October 28, its first hike since 2023.

Jessica Rickerby, president of the Canadian Mortgage Brokers Association of Ontario (CMBA Ontario) in Toronto, said after that move: “While inflation is a key concern of Ontarians, so is housing affordability. The difference is that affordability is a pressing issue right now, whereas inflation is — at present — a hypothetical.”

Who could lead the Bank next — and what it means for brokers

The Bank’s 14-page executive brief for the role sets a high bar for candidates.

Applicants must hold Canadian citizenship and a graduate-level degree in economics, speak both official languages at a high level, and bring experience at the most senior levels of central banking, public policy, financial regulation, or international institutions.

The board has partnered with Quebec economists who joined the Bank of Canada’s inner circle in 2026 and other senior policymakers in shaping the institution Macklem leaves behind.

For brokers navigating Canada’s mounting 2026 mortgage renewal pressures, the transition carries direct weight.

Bruno Valko, vice-president of national sales at RMG Mortgage Corporation in Toronto, recently questioned the Bank’s inflation outlook: “Come 2027, when comparing oil prices to 2026, assuming oil continues to hover around $100 per barrel, I dispute the rationale around how inflation can average 3% when it’s currently 3.1%.”

items.title: Canada housing starts can absorb Budget 2026 growth, gap persists
items.description: New immigration levels won’t overwhelm housing, but Canada’s supply gap stands at 571,000 units
items.content: <p>New immigration levels won’t overwhelm housing, but Canada’s supply gap stands at 571,000 units</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639304410184682267.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: New immigration levels won’t overwhelm housing, but Canada’s supply gap stands at 571,000 units
items.body:
Canada’s residential construction sector is running at a pace sufficient to absorb projected 2027 population growth under the federal government’s new immigration plan, but a supply deficit built during the 2022–2024 surge will take years to clear.

That is the central finding of a new analysis by Rentals.ca, which used Statistics Canada population estimates alongside Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) housing starts and completions data to establish an absorption benchmark.

“At the current pace of about 240,000 starts a year, absorption capacity is approximately 500,000 people,” the report said, based on the ratio that kept supply aligned with population from 1990 to 2015.

Budget 2026 introduced a new immigration levels plan for 2027 to 2029, setting permanent resident admissions at 380,000 annually and adding up to 282,000 one-time and time-limited transitions alongside 370,000 new temporary resident arrivals.

Because most transitions target individuals already residing in Canada, net population growth will be narrower than the headline figures imply.

The report said projected 2027 population growth of 177,000 to 440,000 falls below the 500,000-person absorption capacity of current construction in every scenario modelled.

Kevin Fettig of CMI Financial Group says Budget 2026's housing reforms could improve access to financing for smaller developers, but municipal zoning and approval delays must also be addressed to boost supply. https://t.co/KjzLNLNcY7 — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 11, 2026

The gap left by the 2022–2024 surge

The near-term outlook does not resolve Canada’s deeper structural challenge. The cumulative supply gap — measuring units required above those started to maintain historical construction-to-population ratios — peaked at approximately 780,000 units in mid-2024.

“With population growth slowing and starts holding near 240,000 a year, the gap narrowed to about 571,000 units as of mid-2026,” the report said.

As CMHC’s Fall 2026 Housing Supply Report showed, Canada still requires an estimated 187,000 to 238,000 additional units per year beyond current construction to restore affordability.

Closing the existing deficit under the lowest-growth scenario would take nearly four years of construction above population requirements; under the high-growth scenario, more than a decade.

Construction slowdown may delay rent relief

The report said average national asking rents have declined on an annual basis for 25 consecutive months and are down 5.4% over two years, while the national purpose-built rental vacancy rate climbed to 3.1% in 2025, above its 10-year average.

That cushion is already narrowing: “Asking rents in Toronto and Vancouver are rising for the first time in nearly three years, and the collapse in condo presales will reduce completions in 2028 and 2029,” the report said.

Mathieu Laberge, Chief Economist and Senior Vice President at CMHC in Ottawa, addressed the construction risk directly at the recent Mortgage Professionals Canada National conference in Calgary.

“If we react to a softer market by stopping too much construction, we may be protecting ourselves from today’s risks — but we’re also creating tomorrow’s shortages,” he warned.

“We are at a very high risk that by not providing the appropriate and sufficient supply today, we will lose the improvement in affordability we’ve seen two or three, or five years down the road.”

Laberge also pointed to a structural mismatch in what is being built: “Canada doesn’t simply have too much or too little housing. The reality is that we have a mismatch between the homes people need and the homes the system is producing. What’s small is unaffordable and what’s large is unavailable.”

For brokers advising clients on purchase timing and rental strategy, the report cautioned that newly permanent residents are likely to accelerate household formation, pushing vacancy rates lower before the pipeline fully catches up.

“Pressure on rents and vacancy rates that built up during the surge is therefore likely to ease more gradually than previously projected,” it said.

The bottom line for brokers

The report is broadly constructive in one sense — 2027 isn’t going to see a repeat of the 2022–2024 demand shock. But it is not a signal that the structural supply problem is solved.

The practical read for brokers is that the market remains undersupplied relative to long-run need, rent relief is fragile, and a new cohort of newly permanent residents is about to start forming households and entering the mortgage market.

Getting in front of that client segment now, while also managing the renewal and purchase conversations shaped by a persistent gap, is where the opportunity sits.

items.title: Commission scheme costs former BC realtor his licence and $627,000
items.description: Regulator details kickbacks, a fake inspection and deleted emails behind the penalty
items.content: <p>Regulator details kickbacks, a fake inspection and deleted emails behind the penalty</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0311_638563834459414345.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Regulator details kickbacks, a fake inspection and deleted emails behind the penalty
items.body:
A former Squamish, BC, real estate agent who funnelled buyers to two colleagues in exchange for kickbacks must pay $627,000.

The BC Financial Services Authority (BCFSA) also cancelled his licence in a sanctions decision dated Oct. 28 and made public Nov. 13.

The order against Andre Zubko and his personal real estate corporation stems from a commission scheme he ran across eight home sales in 2016 and 2017. It combines $320,000 in discipline penalties with $307,000 in enforcement expenses.

Zubko’s licence renewal was denied in 2017, and he has not been licensed since.

How did the commission scheme work?

Zubko was licensed from 2006 to 2017 and worked at One Percent Realty, a flat-fee brokerage.

According to the decision, he sent unrepresented buyers to a high school acquaintance and to a cousin of a family member. Those agents wrote offers demanding a higher buyer’s commission, then passed most of it back to him.

Sellers paid more than $50,000 in extra commissions, and Zubko collected $47,641.23 in kickbacks.

Two deals went further. In one, Zubko persuaded a seller to cut the price of a lot sold to his family member from $350,000 to $175,000. The contract was assigned days later for $335,000, a $160,000 gain.

In another, he invented a home inspection to push a price down from $807,000 to $797,000, even though he knew the contract had already been assigned for $845,000.

“It is difficult to imagine a more clear-cut case of deception of one’s client than completely making up a negative home inspection in order to convince that client to sell their property at a lower price,” Senior Hearing Officer Andrew Pendray wrote.

During the investigation, Zubko deleted emails, met with others involved to align their accounts, and gave investigators false statements.

Canadian Mortgage Professional reported the regulator’s original misconduct findings in 2024. 

FSRA's has permanently removed a former mortgage agent's licence and imposed administrative penalties after findings related to unlicensed mortgage activity, improper compensation arrangements, and facilitating dishonesty. https://t.co/Wjos9A5fUi — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 3, 2026

What the penalty signals for BC brokers

Four transactions fell under the rules in force before Sept. 30, 2016, which capped penalties at $10,000.

For the remaining four, Pendray assessed $550,000, then cut it by 50% to $275,000. He cited proportionality and Zubko’s years without a licence.

He added $35,000 to strip out any remaining profit and set enforcement costs at 65% of the regulator’s expenses.

Zubko had proposed about $85,000 in penalties and $40,000 in costs.

Limiting fines to client losses, Pendray wrote, would turn them into “just the cost of doing business in an inappropriate way, and only if one was caught.”

The ruling lands weeks after BC’s Mortgage Services Act took effect on Oct. 13, completing the province’s overhaul of mortgage broker regulation.

The regulator has also acted against individual brokers, including one barred for falsifying clients’ income records. 

Zubko has 30 days from the decision to appeal to the Financial Services Tribunal and 60 days to pay.

items.title: October inflation steady, complicating BoC’s December call
items.description: Canada’s October CPI held flat, raising doubts over another Bank of Canada rate hike
items.content: <p>Canada’s October CPI held flat, raising doubts over another Bank of Canada rate hike</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639304381242559284.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Canada’s October CPI held flat, raising doubts over another Bank of Canada rate hike
items.body:
Canada’s annual inflation rate held at 3.1% in October, matching September’s reading and coming in just below the 3.2% most economists had expected. The data has now tilted the debate toward a potential pause at the Bank of Canada’s (BoC) December 9 rate decision.

Statistics Canada reported Monday that the consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.2% on a seasonally adjusted basis month over month in October.

Upward pressure from gasoline, groceries, clothing, and natural gas was partially offset by cheaper cell phone plans and slower rent growth.

Excluding energy, the CPI rose 2.0% year over year, edging down from 2.1% in September.

Gasoline remained the dominant inflationary driver, rising 30.9% year over year from 27.8% in September, reflecting a base-year effect tied to lower crude oil prices in October 2025.

Despite that headline figure, pump prices fell 2.5% month over month. Grocery price growth ticked up to 2.0% year over year from 1.7%, breaking a four-month easing streak, with fresh vegetable prices rising 1.4% after declining 2.9% in September.

Clothing costs climbed 1.8% year over year, the largest monthly increase since September 2019, with Statistics Canada attributing the move to higher shipping costs.

Excluding food and energy, the CPI eased to 1.8% year over year.

Canada’s labour market shed 4,700 jobs in October, pushing the national unemployment rate to 6.7% from 6.5%, a third consecutive month of deterioration that is now complicating the Bank of Canada’s (BoC) path to a December rate hike. https://t.co/M8Ce4IYrjH — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 10, 2026

Economists split on December

The BoC’s preferred core measures — CPI-trim at 1.8% and CPI-median at 2.0% year over year — held at or below the 2% target. The case for holding at December 9 has strengthened, though the question is not fully settled.

Andrew Grantham, senior economist at CIBC Economics in Toronto, was direct: “Today’s tame inflation report, combined with the recent move lower in gasoline prices and signs of weakness in the labour market, suggest that there’s no need for the Bank of Canada to rush another interest rate hike and supports our call for a hold in December.”

RBC Economics’ Abbey Xu, based in Toronto, retained a more cautious outlook. Her base case remains a 25-basis-point hike to 2.75% at the December meeting, “although further downside surprises in growth, employment or inflation could still give policymakers reason to pause.”

Leslie Preston, senior economist at TD Economics in Toronto, characterised the BoC’s October 28 move to 2.5% as pre-emptive: “The Bank of Canada raised interest rates in October to get ahead of an expected uptick in inflation in Canada, but the signs of hotter price gains were fairly lukewarm in October.”

What it means for brokers

Bond yields and the Canadian dollar both fell Monday following the release, signalling that markets are trimming expectations of a December hike.

For mortgage professionals across Canada, the December 9 announcement will carry unusual weight for client conversations and product strategy.

Three consecutive monthly job losses, softer-than-expected third-quarter GDP growth, and declining gasoline prices, as flagged by RBC’s Xu, now all argue for patience from the BoC.

Whether core inflation broadens enough over the next three weeks to justify another rate increase will determine whether Canada’s mortgage market greets 2027 at 2.5% or 2.75%.

Time for your cheat sheet on this week’s top stories.

Canadian Real Estate

Canadian Immigration Changes To Double Population Growth Rate: BMO

Canada’s looking to boost its immigration, but it hasn’t framed it that way. Officially, the target is to add 380,000 new permanent residents per year for 2027-29. However, BMO economists estimate that special measures push the total to 660,000 for 2027. The massive change has the bank nearly doubling its population growth forecast. Though it’s worth distinguishing between a target and reality. Canada’s foreign student tapering only began after applications dropped sharply, suggesting exhausted demand.

Canadian Housing Affordability’s Record Recovery May End Soon: NBF

Housing affordability across Canada has made a record 11 straight quarters of improvement. That sounds impressive, but the details are less flattering. Mortgage payments on a typical home would consume 50.9% of a median household’s income at this level. Even with the record length of improvements, this is still one of the worst markets for buyers in history. National Bank economists warn this may also be as good as it gets in the near-term, as mortgage rates are set to climb.

Canada To Add 200,000 Permanent Resident Spots, Housing Boost Limited

Canada’s immigration plan will boost permanent residents 50% higher than the headline data suggests. It’s seen as a boost to the economy, especially housing demand, but that may not be the case. The added capacity targets those already in the country and looking to stay. While this can mean less churn and ultimately more people, demand doesn’t get a direct boost. Their consumption is already reflected in the current data.

Ontario Real Estate

Ontario Property Tax Arrears Hit 24-Year High, Brampton Leads At 11.9%

Ontario property tax arrears are at a 24-year high, driven by Toronto’s suburbs. Filings show the property tax arrears rate hit 7.2% of the $34.1 billion in levies for 2025, up 2.46 points since 2019. The rate is now at its highest level since 2001, but there’s an important distinction here. Today, the rate is climbing, but back then it was falling after the early ‘90s real estate bubble popped. Coincidentally, property taxes just made their biggest increase since the early ’90s.

Toronto Real Estate

Over 1 In 8 Greater Toronto Rental Units Sit Vacant As Completions Hit A Record

Greater Toronto’s rental construction boom means a lot of supply is sitting empty. The often-reported vacancy rate for stabilized purpose-built rentals fell from 5.4% to 3.0% in Q3. The catch is stabilized, which excludes buildings that have never hit 95% occupancy. In a normal market, it may not be a big difference; including all purpose-built units means a 13.3% vacancy rate. Even with 1 in 8 units vacant, there are 34,545 more currently under construction, nearly half of the units being built across Canada. So far, there’s been minimal progress on prices, but that can change fast with a record supply glut on the way.
